_about: Every entry is a real publication whose existence was confirmed by a web search on verifiedOn. 'finding' is a plain-language summary written for coaching use, hedged to what the paper supports. Never add an entry without a verifiedUrl.

entries.citation: Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210.
entries.finding: People paid only $1 to tell the next participant a dull task was fun later rated the task as more enjoyable than people paid $20. With little outside justification, the mind changed the belief to match the behavior.
entries.caveat: Single 1959 lab study. Dissonance as a mechanism has been replicated and refined many times, but the original sample was small.

entries.citation: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119.
entries.finding: Deciding in advance exactly when, where and how you will act ('If situation X happens, I will do Y') raised goal attainment with a medium-to-large average effect.
entries.caveat: Effects are strongest for goals the person already wants. It does not create motivation.

entries.citation: Oettingen, G. (2012). Future thought and behaviour change. European Review of Social Psychology, 23(1), 1-63.
entries.design: Narrative review of the author's lab and field work
entries.finding: Picturing the wish and then the real obstacle in your way (mental contrasting), paired with an if-then plan, shifts commitment to match how winnable the goal is: more effort when it is realistic, an earlier, cleaner release when it is not.
entries.caveat: Review by the originator of the method. Independent replications are still accumulating.

entries.citation: Nolen-Hoeksema, S., Wisco, B. E., & Lyubomirsky, S. (2008). Rethinking rumination. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 3(5), 400-424.
entries.finding: Repetitive, passive focus on your distress and its causes is linked to depression, to worse problem solving, and to staying stuck. Active, concrete problem solving is not the same thing.
entries.caveat: Mostly correlational and longitudinal evidence. Coaching is not treatment for depression; refer out when clients describe it.

entries.citation: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998-1009.
entries.finding: Reaching automatic behavior took a median of 66 days, with a very wide range between people and behaviors. One missed day did not wreck the habit curve.
entries.caveat: Small sample, self-reported automaticity, simple behaviors. '21 days' is a myth; do not repeat it.

entries.citation: Bryan, C. J., Walton, G. M., Rogers, T., & Dweck, C. S. (2011). Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(31), 12653-12656.
entries.design: Randomized field experiments around real elections
entries.finding: Wording that framed voting as being a person ('be a voter') rather than doing an act ('vote') increased turnout. Identity language can move behavior more than task language.
entries.caveat: Voting is a one-time, socially visible act. Do not assume the same size of effect for daily habits.

entries.citation: Cohen, G. L., & Sherman, D. K. (2014). The psychology of change: Self-affirmation and social psychological intervention. Annual Review of Psychology, 65, 333-371.
entries.finding: Reflecting on core values you hold makes people less defensive when they face threatening information, and open to change they would otherwise resist.
entries.caveat: Effects are often small and context-dependent. Authors are the main proponents of the theory.

entries.citation: Sheldon, K. M., & Elliot, A. J. (1999). Goal striving, need satisfaction, and longitudinal well-being: The self-concordance model. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 76(3), 482-497.
entries.finding: Goals pursued for reasons that are truly your own got more sustained effort and were reached more often, and reaching them lifted well-being. Goals chased out of guilt or pressure did not give the same return.
entries.caveat: Student samples, self-report. Consistent with later self-determination research.

entries.citation: Yeager, D. S., et al. (2019). A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement. Nature, 573, 364-369.
entries.design: Preregistered randomized trial, nationally representative US sample of 9th graders
entries.finding: A brief online growth-mindset program improved grades for lower-achieving students and raised enrollment in advanced math overall, with the benefit concentrated in schools whose peers supported challenge-seeking.
entries.caveat: Effects were small and conditional on context. A mindset belief alone is not a strategy; pair it with specific action.

entries.citation: Hagger, M. S., et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573.
entries.finding: A large coordinated replication found an ego-depletion effect near zero. Do not tell clients that willpower is a tank that runs dry.
entries.caveat: This does not prove depletion never happens; the field is still debating. Use as a guardrail against overclaiming, not as the headline.

entries.citation: Oettingen, G., & Mayer, D. (2002). The motivating function of thinking about the future: Expectations versus fantasies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1198-1212.
entries.design: Four longitudinal studies (job seekers, students with a crush, an intro psychology class, hip-replacement patients), roughly 40 to 117 follow-ups each
entries.finding: Believing a good outcome is likely predicted more effort and better results. Dwelling on vivid, pleasant fantasies of the outcome predicted less effort and worse results across the four studies. In the exam study, effort partly explained the link.
entries.caveat: Small samples, mostly correlational follow-ups. The idea is that fantasy alone can feel like having arrived; it does not say never to picture success.

entries.citation: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68-78.
entries.finding: People are more self-motivated and do better when three needs are supported: autonomy, competence and relatedness. When those needs are blocked, motivation and well-being fall. Context shapes whether someone feels engaged or alienated.
entries.caveat: A theory paper that summarizes a research program, not a single test. Broad cross-cultural support, but 'needs' is still debated in detail.

entries.citation: Breines, J. G., & Chen, S. (2012). Self-compassion increases self-improvement motivation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 38(9), 1133-1143.
entries.finding: After thinking about a weakness or a failure, people who were prompted to treat themselves with self-compassion believed they could improve, studied longer after failing a hard test, and were more motivated to change, compared with control groups.
entries.caveat: Lab experiments with short-term measures, often student samples. Self-compassion here means acceptance plus improvement, not letting yourself off the hook.
